title: Sex-Related Differences in Chronic Pain: A Narrative Review by a Multidisciplinary Task Force
authors: Maurizio Marchesini; Diego Fornasari; Silvia Natoli; Elena Vegni; Arturo Cuomo; Allison B. Reiss
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain, including low back pain, osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, migraines, neuropathic pain, chronic pelvic pain, and others.
context_note: Italian context: Censis-Grünenthal survey and Italian National Institute of Health survey data cited.
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the biopsychosocial label as a rationale for personalized, interdisciplinary pain management, but does not define the model or operationalize it. It reviews biological, psychological, and social factors separately without integrating them mechanistically.
integration_mechanism_summary: No cross-domain pathways are proposed. The paper lists biological, psychological, and social factors as parallel contributors to sex differences in chronic pain, with only descriptive associations (e.g., SES associated with pain severity).
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper claims factors interact but provides no mechanistic pathways
conceptual_tensions_2: BPS model is invoked as a solution but never defined or operationalized
conceptual_tensions_3: Sex and gender are distinguished conceptually but often conflated in the review's own language
additional_observations_1: The review is structured by domain (biological, psycho-social, pharmacological) with no cross-domain synthesis
additional_observations_2: Psychological constructs (catastrophizing, depression, anxiety) are named but not defined or measured
additional_observations_3: Social factors are more elaborated than in many BPS reviews, including gender biases, SES, and cultural roles
synthesis_note: This narrative review provides a comprehensive list of sex-related biological, psychological, and social factors in chronic pain, but treats them as parallel contributors. The BPS label is used rhetorically to justify personalized care, with no integration mechanisms or definition of the model. Psychological constructs are named but undefined.
coding_rationale: Typology 'multifactorial' because all three domains are substantively present but treated in parallel. Triadic integration 'partial' because bio-psych and psych-social have descriptive links, but bio-social is only mentioned. BPS label is undefined and used as intervention rationale.

title: Sex-Related Differences in Chronic Pain: A Narrative Review by a Multidisciplinary Task Force
authors: Maurizio Marchesini; Diego Fornasari; Silvia Natoli; Elena Vegni; Arturo Cuomo; Allison B. Reiss
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (CP), defined as pain persisting for over 3 months, with sex-related differences in prevalence, perception, and treatment response.
context_note: Italian expert task force; prevalence examples from Italy and Western countries.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS by listing sex and gender differences, symptoms, physiological indicators, medical history, lifestyle, and psychological aspects as factors to consider, then organizing evidence into biological, psycho-social, treatment, and adverse-drug sections. It rarely specifies cross-domain pathways.
integration_mechanism_summary: No explicit cross-domain mechanism is specified. The review repeatedly states that biological, psycho-social, and socio-economic factors interact and influence pain experiences, treatment response, and outcomes, but it does not name a mediator or pathway.
conceptual_tensions_1: Sex and gender are explicitly conflated while the review calls for a more nuanced understanding of both
conceptual_tensions_2: BPS is invoked as operational, but the paper lists factors without formally defining the model or specifying cross-domain mechanisms
conceptual_tensions_3: Women constitute the majority of CP sufferers, yet research and clinical trials are described as historically male-biased
conceptual_tensions_4: Sex-specific analgesic and opioid findings are mixed and attributed to differences in experimental design, pain stimulus type, and sample size
conceptual_tensions_5: Psychological therapy is recommended, but patients may misunderstand it as implying pain is psychosomatic or “in their head”
additional_observations_1: The review is narrative and expert-driven, with literature critically appraised but no formal risk-of-bias or quality tool named
additional_observations_2: The paper uses both “psycho-social” and “biopsychosocial,” but the hyphenated psycho-social term is more common in the body
additional_observations_3: Treatment sections emphasize pharmacology, adverse drug reactions, pharmacokinetics, and sex-disaggregated trial data more than psychosocial care
additional_observations_4: The paper reports sex-disaggregated prevalence and outcomes but does not pool evidence or provide effect estimates
additional_observations_5: Lifestyle appears only as a BPS component in the abstract and is not elaborated substantively
additional_observations_6: Care settings span clinical practice, pain clinics, pain rehabilitation programs, clinical trials, and population surveys
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly by listing sex/gender, biological, psycho-social, and socio-economic factors and organizing evidence into sex-difference sections. It offers several directional associations (SES, mental health, support, treatment response) but little named mechanism. Overall, it is a descriptive true-integrative narrative with bio-psych emphasis and social content mostly as modifiers of care and outcomes.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is substantive but thinner. Triadic integration is descriptive, not mechanistic; BPS is used to organize and justify sex-aware care.

title: Sex-Related Differences in Chronic Pain: A Narrative Review by a Multidisciplinary Task Force
authors: Maurizio Marchesini; Diego Fornasari; Silvia Natoli; Elena Vegni; Arturo Cuomo; Allison B. Reiss
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain with sex-related differences, focusing on prevalence, mechanisms, and treatment response in women and men.
context_note: Italian population-based surveys (Censis-Grünenthal and Italian National Institute of Health) provide epidemiological data.
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework to structure discussion of sex differences in chronic pain, integrating biological, psychological, and social factors without specifying mechanistic pathways between domains.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper asserts that biological, psychological, and social factors interact in complex ways but does not specify the mechanisms or pathways of these interactions
conceptual_tensions_2: While the BPS model is presented as integrating multiple domains, the review discusses them in parallel without demonstrating how they causally relate to each other
additional_observations_1: The review emphasizes sex differences but does not explicitly address gender as a distinct social construct from biological sex
additional_observations_2: The paper recommends sex-aware clinical practices but does not provide specific operational definitions for how to implement BPS principles in practice
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses the biopsychosocial model as an organizing framework to discuss sex differences in chronic pain, covering biological (hormonal, genetic, neuroimmune), psychological (catastrophizing, depression, anxiety), and social (SES, gender biases, employment) factors. However, it does not propose mechanistic pathways between domains, treating them as parallel rather than integrated. The review's strength lies in its comprehensive identification of sex-specific risk factors across all three BPS domains, while its limitation is the absence of explicit integration mechanisms.
coding_rationale: BPS typology is 'multifactorial' because all three domains are substantively present but treated in parallel without specified integration mechanisms. Domain coverage is 'elaborated' for all three core domains based on multiple named constructs. Integration is 'none' because no cross-domain pathways are specified despite the paper's assertion of interaction.
